subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 6 · The Torchbearer — Charismatic and Transformational Leadership

questions.stem: Describe Weber's charisma.
options: A form of influence based on followers' perceptions that the leader is endowed with exceptional qualities — granted by followers, often in a crisis
Authority from tradition — followers obey because the leader's family or office has always been obeyed in that society
Authority from the rules — followers obey because the law and the organisation's written procedures give the leader the formal right to command them
A fixed personality trait that some leaders are born with and that cannot be developed, lost or transferred to others

questions.stem: Identify the locus of charismatic leadership, according to the textbook.
options: All three — the leader, the followers and the situation; it is a relationship
The leader only — charisma is a quality of the person that followers simply recognise
The followers only — charisma is whatever the followers decide to attribute to the leader
The situation only — any leader becomes charismatic when a crisis demands one
questions.why: Remove any one and the charisma fades. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Explain why the locus matters.
options: Because charisma is a relationship, it can be built — and lost when the situation changes or followers stop attributing
It proves that charisma is inherited, because the leader's exceptional qualities exist before the followers ever arrive
It shows that charisma is permanent, because once followers attribute it they do not withdraw it
It has no practical use, because leaders cannot control the followers or the situation

questions.stem: Identify Weber's three bases of authority.
options: Charismatic, traditional and rational-legal
Position power, personal power and expert power
Trait, behaviour and situation
Reward, coercive, legitimate and referent

questions.stem: Identify effects charismatic leaders have on followers.
options: Trust in the leader's beliefs, unquestioning acceptance, willing obedience, emotional involvement, heightened goals, increased confidence and effort
Boredom and compliance, with followers doing exactly what is asked and nothing more, and leaving the organisation as soon as a better job appears elsewhere
Independence from the leader, with followers making their own decisions without reference to the vision
Lower goals, because followers rely on the leader to achieve the difficult things for them
questions.why: Every one can serve the followers or the leader alone. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Describe how charismatic qualities can be acquired.
options: Develop visionary skills, be candid and take a stand, build enthusiasm with stories and symbols, develop empathy, take risks and be seen to sacrifice
They cannot — charisma is a gift that followers recognise in some leaders and not in others, and no amount of training, coaching or practice can create it in anyone
Only by promotion to a position senior enough for followers to attribute exceptional qualities
Only by winning, because followers attribute charisma to leaders who have succeeded
questions.why: Most of it is behaviour. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Identify the textbook's caution about the effects on followers.
options: Every one of them can serve the followers or the leader alone
They always help the organisation, because committed followers produce better results
They never last, because followers withdraw the attribution as soon as the crisis passes
They only appear in politics, where crowds attribute qualities to leaders they have never met

questions.stem: Explain what the chapter asks about founders described as charismatic.
options: Which acquired qualities can be observed in their speeches and decisions, and which are attributed after success
Whether they are rich enough to have built their companies without needing charisma to attract investors or employees
Whether they are famous enough for their charisma to be studied
Whether they are tall, since height is one of the traits associated with charisma

questions.stem: Identify the one question that separates socialised from personalised charismatic leaders.
options: Whose needs does the leader's power serve?
How loud and confident is the leader when speaking?
How many followers does the leader have?
How old was the leader when the followers first appeared?

questions.stem: Describe how a personalised charismatic leader responds to criticism.
options: Punishes, isolates critics, rewrites history
Listens, adjusts the plan and admits mistakes in public
Ignores it politely and continues with the plan
Holds a vote so that the followers can decide

questions.stem: Describe the succession pattern of a socialised charismatic leader.
options: Builds leaders who can replace them
Ensures that nobody can replace them, so that the organisation depends on them
Leaves no plan, because succession is the board's responsibility
Appoints a relative, so that the leader's vision is kept in the family

questions.stem: Identify the four things followers should watch to tell the two types apart.
options: Who benefits, whether questions are welcome, whether the leader admits error, and whether others are being developed
Salary, car, office, title, bonus, holiday entitlement and the number of staff who report directly to the leader at head office
Age, height, voice and dress
Speeches, awards, press coverage and fans

questions.stem: Describe transactional leadership.
options: An exchange — contingent reward and management by exception — that maintains stability
Changing the status quo with a compelling vision that moves followers beyond self-interest
Serving followers' growth so that they become healthier, wiser and freer
Charisma granted by followers who perceive exceptional qualities in the leader

questions.stem: Describe transformational leadership.
options: Raises followers' awareness of the importance of outcomes, moves them beyond self-interest and activates higher-order needs
Pays exactly on target and intervenes only when results slip below the standard, so that followers know exactly what to expect
Acts only when things go wrong and otherwise leaves followers to the routine
Keeps everything stable so that followers know exactly what to expect
questions.why: Followers do more than they thought they could. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Explain the textbook's position on the two.
options: They are not opposites — the best leaders do both: transactional to run the organisation, transformational to change it
Choose one approach and stay with it, because followers are confused and lose trust in a leader who switches between the two styles
Transactional leadership is obsolete, because modern followers want meaning rather than exchange
Transformational leadership is dangerous, because it depends on charisma that can be misused

questions.stem: Explain the limit of transactional leadership.
options: It gets what it pays for and no more
It costs too much, because every contribution has to be rewarded
It is illegal in many countries, which restrict performance-related pay
It needs charisma, which most transactional leaders do not have

questions.stem: Identify the four stages of the transformation process in order.
options: Make a compelling case for change; inspire a shared vision; lead the transition; implant the change
Write the vision; set the budget; launch the programme; review the results
Hire the right people; train them; reward them; promote the best
Plan the change in detail; organise the teams; lead the people through it; control the results against the plan
questions.why: Skipping a stage is the usual cause of a transformation that fades. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Describe stage 4.
options: Institutionalise the change — align structures, rewards and culture so the change outlasts the leader
Raise sensitivity to environmental threats and opportunities so that followers see the need for change
Express the vision in ideological terms so that followers find meaning in it
Instil a sense of urgency and build teams to carry the change through

questions.stem: Explain why the textbook calls Oprah transformational, not only charismatic.
options: Stages 3–4 took two years of restructuring before the 2013 turnaround — transformation is measured by what changed
She is famous enough for her leadership to be studied in a textbook and quoted in management courses around the world
She made speeches that inspired her audience and her staff
Her audience loved her and attributed exceptional qualities to her

questions.stem: Identify what happens without 'felt need' in stage 1.
options: Nothing moves
The vision carries it anyway
Stage 2 replaces it
The change implants itself
questions.why: Without felt need, nothing moves. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four transformational behaviours.
options: Idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration
Directive, supportive, participative and achievement-oriented — the four styles of the path–goal theory from chapter 4
Decide, consult, facilitate and delegate
Plan, do, check and act

questions.stem: Describe intellectual stimulation.
options: Questioning assumptions, reframing problems, encouraging followers to think and challenge — including the leader
Being a role model whom followers admire, trust and want to emulate in their own behaviour and in the way they treat others
A compelling vision, high expectations and optimism about the future
Attention to each follower's needs for achievement and growth

questions.stem: Differentiate charismatic from transformational leadership.
options: Charisma is one dimension (idealised influence); a charismatic leader need not transform anything and a transformational leader need not be charismatic
They are identical, and the textbook uses the two words for the same kind of leader in different chapters simply to avoid repeating the same word too often on one page
Charisma is broader, because it covers all four transformational behaviours and more
Transformation needs no vision, because it is measured by what changed in the structure
questions.why: Transformation is measured by what changed. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Identify the power base of transformational leaders.
options: Relational — referent and expert, not position
Legitimate and coercive power from the position
Reward power only, because transformation is paid for
Connection power only, because transformation needs allies

questions.stem: Describe stewardship.
options: Employee-focused leadership that empowers followers to decide and control their jobs; the leader holds the organisation in trust
Leadership by exchange, in which followers receive rewards for meeting the leader's targets and penalties when they fall short of them
Leadership by charisma, in which followers attribute exceptional qualities to the leader
Leadership by pressure, in which followers comply because the leader can punish them

questions.stem: Identify the test of servant leadership.
options: Do the served grow — healthier, wiser, freer, more likely to become servants themselves?
Are the served comfortable and content with how they are treated?
Does the leader get credit for the results the followers produce?
Is the leader obeyed willingly by the followers without ever having to use position power or threats?

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'does serving followers mean obeying them?'.
options: No — a servant leader serves the underperformer with honest feedback and serves the team by stopping the bully; service is measured by growth, not comfort
Yes — the followers decide everything, and the servant leader simply carries out their decisions whether or not they are wise, because service means obedience
Yes — comfort is the goal, because followers who are comfortable perform better
No — servants never give feedback, because feedback is a form of control

questions.stem: Identify the stewardship attributes.
options: Team orientation, decentralised decisions, equality assumptions, rewards shared with those who create them
Centralised control, with every decision taken at the top and the rewards reserved for the leader and the senior team around them
Vision and charisma that followers attribute to the leader
Management by exception and contingent reward

questions.stem: Identify step 3 of the diagnosis sequence.
options: Socialised or personalised? — who benefits, whether criticism is welcome, whether successors are built
Which stage of transformation is the organisation in, and how long has it been there under the current leader?
Is there evidence of service and stewardship?
Do followers attribute exceptional qualities to the leader?

questions.stem: Describe the one-sentence judgement at the end of the sequence.
options: This leader is [charismatic / transformational / transactional / a mix], serving [the followers / themselves], at stage [n] — with the evidence
This leader is good or bad, judged by the financial results of the organisation over the period the leader has been in charge of it and by nothing else at all
This leader is popular, judged by what the followers say
This leader is rich, judged by the rewards the position carries

questions.stem: Identify an effect on followers that signals a personalised leader when combined with silence.
options: Unquestioning acceptance and dependence
Higher goals set by the followers
Trust in the leader's beliefs
Emulation of the leader's behaviour and values

questions.stem: Identify the Maslow needs transformational leaders activate.
options: Esteem and self-actualisation
Physiological and safety
Belongingness only
None — transformation bypasses needs

questions.stem: Exercise 1A: the hospital director whose staff say 'she made us believe this hospital could be the best in the region' and who coaches junior doctors every Thursday. Classify the leader.
options: Transformational — inspirational motivation plus individualised consideration; socialised
Transactional — she rewards the doctors who meet her targets and intervenes only when something goes wrong on a ward
Personalised charismatic — the staff adore her
Steward only — she holds the hospital in trust
questions.why: Answer key: A transformational, socialised. See §6.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1B: the sales director who pays exactly on target, intervenes only when numbers slip, and whose team is stable, competent and uninspired. Classify the leader.
options: Transactional — contingent reward and management by exception
Transformational — his team is stable because he has changed it
Socialised charismatic — his team trusts him
Servant — he serves the team by intervening only when needed
questions.why: Answer key: B transactional. See §6.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1C: the adored founder who takes credit for every idea, fired the last three deputies, and whose company nobody can imagine without him. Classify the leader.
options: Personalised charismatic — credit-taking, no successors, dependence
Socialised charismatic — the company depends on him because he serves it
Transformational — he has transformed the company around himself
Steward — he holds the company in trust
questions.why: Answer key: C personalised charismatic. See §6.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1D: the school principal who moved decisions to teachers, shares every award with the staff, and is called 'the person who made me a better teacher'. Classify the leader.
options: Steward/servant — decentralised decisions, shared rewards; the served grow
Transactional — he rewards teachers who improve
Personalised charismatic — the teachers adore him
Charismatic only — the teachers attribute exceptional qualities to him and follow him
questions.why: Answer key: D steward/servant. See §6.7 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1E: the minister with a compelling vision, a national audience and a reform programme that stalled after the speeches. Classify the leader and determine the stage skipped.
options: Charismatic — stages 3–4 skipped: vision without transition or implanting
Transformational — stage 4 is complete because the vision was shared nationally
Transactional — stage 1 was skipped because the case for change was never made
Servant — stage 2 was skipped because the vision was the minister's alone
questions.why: Answer key: E charismatic, stages 3–4 skipped. See §6.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Determine the strongest of the four behaviours in Exercise 1A (the hospital director).
options: Individualised consideration
Idealised influence
Intellectual stimulation
Inspirational motivation only
questions.why: Answer key: A strongest — individualised consideration. See §6.6 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1C: Determine two signals the founder's followers should have noticed earlier, and the Chapter 2 dark-side label.
options: Credit-taking and the firing of deputies (no successors) — narcissism
Long hours and constant travel between the company's offices — conscientiousness
Speeches and awards — surgency
Shared rewards with the team — stewardship
questions.why: Answer key, task 3. See §6.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: a founder's profile shows staff saying 'he saved us when the bank called in the loan'. Determine the step and the reading.
options: Step 1 — followers attribute exceptional qualities and the situation (a crisis) called for a saviour: charisma present
Step 4 — transactional leadership, because the founder exchanged job security for the loyalty and silence of the staff during the crisis
Step 7 — stewardship, because the founder held the company in trust during the crisis
Step 6 — intellectual stimulation, because the founder found a new way to pay the loan
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §6.8 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: the profile shows the founder admits mistakes publicly, welcomes challenge in meetings and has promoted two deputies to run divisions. Determine the classification.
options: Socialised charismatic — benefit to the group, openness to criticism, successors built
Personalised charismatic — the deputies were promoted to protect the founder
Transactional only — the deputies were rewarded for loyalty
Not charismatic — a leader who admits mistakes is not attributed exceptional qualities
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1. See §6.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: the case for change was made, the vision is shared in staff's own words, teams were restructured — but rewards and procedures still reward the old behaviour. Determine the stage and the risk.
options: Stage 3 complete, stage 4 not yet — the change is fragile until implanted
Stage 1 — nothing has really moved because the rewards are unchanged
Stage 4 complete — the restructured teams make the change safe
Stage 2 — the vision is missing because staff describe it in their own words
questions.why: Reward students who note that an unimplanted change is fragile. See §6.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, task 3: the profile shows strong inspiring speeches and role-modelling but no evidence of coaching individuals. Determine the weakest behaviour and the cost if the leader left tomorrow.
options: Individualised consideration is weakest; without developed people, the transformation may collapse with the leader
Idealised influence is weakest; nothing at all would change in the organisation if the leader left tomorrow morning
Inspirational motivation is weakest; morale would rise if the leader left
Intellectual stimulation is weakest; nothing would be lost if the leader left
questions.why: The 'if the leader left' question tests whether transformation or charisma is doing the work. See §6.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select a correctly formatted one-sentence judgement from Exercise 2.
options: 'This leader is transformational with socialised charisma, serving the followers, at stage 3 — the vision is in staff's words but rewards still pay for the old behaviour.'
'This leader is great, and the staff say so whenever they are asked about the changes he has made since he arrived at the company, which shows that the culture has changed.'
'This leader has a big office and many awards, which shows that the board and the industry recognise what he has achieved.'
'This leader is charismatic because he is famous and the staff trust him to lead the company through whatever comes next.'

questions.stem: Exercise 2, task 4: decisions are pushed to branch managers and bonuses are shared with the teams that earned them. Determine the reading.
options: Stewardship — decentralised decisions and shared rewards
Personalised charisma — the branch managers depend on the founder
Management by exception — the founder intervenes only when branches fail
Transactional only — bonuses are exchanged for results
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §6.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Take-away: a student asks the leader 'what did you have to convince people of when you took over?'. Determine the stage this question tests.
options: Stage 1 — the case for change
Stage 2 — the shared vision
Stage 3 — leading the transition
Stage 4 — implanting the change

questions.stem: Take-away: a follower is asked 'what is this organisation trying to become?' and gives the same answer as the leader. Determine what this proves.
options: Stage 2 — a shared vision — happened
Stage 4 is complete and the change is implanted
The leader is personalised and the follower repeats what is safe
Nothing — followers always repeat the leader's words

questions.stem: Take-away: a follower is asked 'how are you different because of working for this person?' and answers 'I run my own team now; three years ago I couldn't speak in a meeting'. Determine the test passed.
options: The servant-leadership test — the served grow — and individualised consideration
The transactional test — the follower was rewarded for performance with a team of her own
The charisma test — the follower attributes exceptional qualities
The stage 1 test — the follower accepted the case for change

questions.stem: Take-away: a follower answers 'he decides everything and he got the credit for last year's award'. Determine the reading.
options: Personalised rather than socialised; no stewardship
Socialised — the leader decides so that the team can concentrate on the work
Transformational stage 4 — the leader's decisions are institutionalised
Servant — the leader serves the team by taking responsibility

questions.stem: The village believed Rami could deliver them because the gang attack was a crisis and he spoke with certainty. Determine the three parts of the locus present.
options: Leader (exceptional qualities attributed), followers (ready to attribute), situation (a crisis calling for a saviour)
Only the leader — Rami's certainty and his confident voice were what made him charismatic to the frightened villagers
Only the situation — any leader would have been followed during the attack
Only the followers — the villagers needed someone to believe in

questions.stem: The Crow chief's gang adore him, never question him, and the gang would collapse without him. Classify him.
options: Personalised charismatic — dependence, no successors, criticism punished
Socialised charismatic — the gang benefits from his leadership
Transformational — he has changed what the gang believes it is for and raised its goals
Steward — he holds the gang in trust for its members
questions.why: Who benefits; are questions welcome? See §6.3.

questions.stem: Rami promises Omar a bigger share of food for each ridge scouted — nothing more. Classify the leadership.
options: Transactional — contingent reward
Transformational — Omar is moved beyond self-interest
Servant — Rami serves Omar's need for food
Charismatic — Omar attributes exceptional qualities to Rami
questions.why: It gets what it pays for and no more. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Rami tells the team: 'We are not four people chasing a gang; we are the reason this valley will sleep safely again.' Classify the behaviour.
options: Inspirational motivation — a compelling vision in ideological terms
Management by exception — Rami intervenes only when morale slips below the level he expects
Intellectual stimulation — Rami is reframing the problem
Contingent reward — Rami promises the valley's gratitude
questions.why: A compelling vision, high expectations, optimism. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Rami asks Noor to challenge his plan every evening and changes it twice because of her. Classify the behaviour.
options: Intellectual stimulation
Idealised influence
Individualised consideration
Transactional exchange
questions.why: Encouraging followers to challenge — including the leader. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Rami lets each follower choose their own task, shares every reward from the villages equally, and asks only whether each of them is growing. Classify the approach.
options: Stewardship and servant leadership
Personalised charisma — the followers depend on Rami's generosity
Transactional leadership — tasks exchanged for rewards
Management by exception — Rami intervenes only when a follower stops growing
questions.why: Decisions pushed down; rewards shared; do the served grow? See §6.7.

questions.stem: Omar keeps failing at the rope work and Rami says nothing to spare his feelings. Determine the chapter's verdict on this 'service'.
options: It fails — servant leadership serves the underperformer with honest feedback, not comfort
It is perfect servant leadership — Rami puts Omar's feelings first and protects him from embarrassment in front of the team
It is transformational — Rami trusts Omar to improve on his own
It is transactional — Rami withholds criticism in exchange for effort
questions.why: Service is measured by growth, not comfort. See §6.7.

questions.stem: Rami has convinced the village it must change and has shared a vision of safe roads, but has not built a guard, trained anyone or changed how the village rewards courage. Determine the stage and what comes next.
options: Stage 2 complete; stages 3 and 4 — lead the transition and implant the change — remain
Stage 4 complete — the village believes in the vision
Stage 1 not started — the village has not yet accepted the case for change at all and still trusts the old defence
All four stages complete — the vision is shared by everyone in the village

questions.stem: Identify step 5 of the diagnosis sequence.
options: Which stage of transformation is the organisation in — case made, vision shared, transition led, change implanted?
Is charisma present — do followers attribute exceptional qualities to the leader, and did they do so before the success?
Is there stewardship — decisions pushed down and rewards shared?
Which of the four transformational behaviours is strongest?

questions.stem: Identify the evidence to look for in step 7.
options: Decisions pushed down, rewards shared, and whether the served grow
Followers' trust, emulation and emotional involvement
A crisis at the time the leader rose to prominence
Exchanges of reward for performance, and intervention by the leader only by exception

questions.stem: The crisis passes, the valley is calm, and the villagers slowly stop treating Rami as special. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: Charisma is a relationship — when the situation no longer calls for a saviour, the attribution fades
Rami lost his traits once the fighting stopped, because courage and vision only exist while there is a battle to fight
The villagers are ungrateful and forget quickly
Charisma was never present — the villagers were simply afraid
questions.why: Remove any one of the three and charisma fades. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Determine what Weber said about where charismatic authority arises.
options: In a crisis or moment of need, when a leader with a compelling vision attracts followers who believe the leader can deliver them
In stable, peaceful times, when followers have the leisure to admire the leader and to notice the qualities that make them special
Only in formal positions, where the office gives the leader the right to be admired
Only by inheritance, when the leader's family has always been followed

questions.stem: Classify the claim 'Rami was simply born with charisma, so he will always have it'.
options: Wrong — if charisma were only in the person it could neither be developed nor lost
Right — charisma is a gift that some leaders have from birth and others never acquire
Right — traits are fixed, so a charismatic leader stays charismatic
Wrong — charisma does not exist and is only a label applied after success

questions.stem: Rami practises describing the freed valley in concrete pictures, takes a public stand against the elders, and shares the risk by walking first. Determine what he is doing.
options: Acquiring charismatic qualities — visionary skill, candour, visible commitment and risk
Transactional leadership — exchanging his own risk for the villagers' loyalty and obedience
Management by exception — acting only when the elders resist
Stewardship — holding the valley in trust for its people
questions.why: How one acquires charismatic qualities. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Rami runs the daily camp with clear exchanges — tasks for food — and uses the evenings to change what the team believes the journey is for. Determine the chapter's verdict.
options: The best leaders do both — transactional to run it, transformational to change it
He should drop the exchanges altogether, because they undermine the vision he is building
He should drop the vision, because exchanges are what keep the team moving
He is confused and should choose one approach and stay with it

questions.stem: Rami, when judging the Crow chief: 'he is charismatic, serving himself, at stage 1, and will leave ruins'. Determine the format being used.
options: The one-sentence judgement of the diagnosis sequence
A BCF statement describing behaviour, consequences and feelings
A vision statement describing what the organisation will become
A coaching conversation aimed at improving performance

questions.stem: Determine where in the sequence a student checks for 'trust, emulation, emotional involvement — or dependence and silence'.
options: Step 2 — which effects on followers are visible
Step 4 — transactional or transformational, judged by the exchanges and the vision
Step 6 — which of the four behaviours
Step 7 — is there service and stewardship

questions.stem: The villagers adopt Rami's views, copy his way of speaking and set themselves goals higher than before. Determine the effects on followers shown.
options: Belief similarity, emulation and heightened goals — effects of a charismatic leader
Transactional exchange — the villagers copy Rami's views in return for his protection against the gang
Dependence only — the villagers cannot think for themselves
Management by exception — Rami corrects the villagers' goals

questions.stem: Determine which acquired quality Rami practises when he tells the story of the freed mill around every campfire, with emotion and a symbol — the mill's key.
options: Building enthusiasm and optimism through emotion, stories and symbols
Taking risks and demonstrating personal commitment to the team's cause
Developing empathy with the followers' fears
Being candid and taking a stand on difficult questions
questions.why: How one acquires charismatic qualities. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a founder whose speeches are praised but who has never been seen to sacrifice anything for the team. Determine which acquired quality is missing.
options: Taking risks and demonstrating personal commitment — being seen to sacrifice
Visionary skill — describing the future in concrete pictures
Enthusiasm — building optimism through emotion, stories and symbols around the campfire
Candour — taking a stand on difficult questions
